speaker: Nick Kokonas
title: Nick Kokonas on Resurrecting Restaurants, Skin in the Game, and Investing
question: During a severe revenue slump, why can selling gift certificates actually worsen a restaurant's financial position?
guest: There was this whole movement around gift certificates—some people even called them 'restaurant bonds' at a 25% discount, which was basically a Groupon. A gift certificate is a liability on your balance sheet. If you take $25,000 from a gift certificate drive or a GoFundMe, do the math on a restaurant with 40 or 50 employees: at $15 an hour for 10 hours a day, you're going to cover maybe one, two, or three days of payroll. If you want to help your local restaurant, buy food from them now. Because if you buy a gift certificate and go use it in four months, they already spent that money four months ago. One of the big problems a lot of restaurants already have is paying for food they bought four weeks ago with next week's revenue, and gift certificates just exacerbate that problem—it's mortgaging their future. A lot of restaurants didn't realize how that shows up on their balance sheet.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
A gift certificate is not really a sale; it is a short-term loan from the customer. The restaurant gets cash now, but takes on a liability (deferred revenue) that it must repay later in food and service.

During a severe slump, that cash is typically spent immediately on rent, payroll and overdue bills. When the certificates are redeemed, the restaurant has to buy ingredients and pay staff to serve those meals while receiving no new cash for them. If redemptions arrive during the fragile recovery period, they displace paying customers and occupy seats, leaving the business with full costs and little incoming cash at exactly the moment it most needs it.

Several things compound the problem. Certificates are often sold at a discount or with bonus value to encourage purchases, so the restaurant owes more than it collected. The cash can also mask how insolvent the business really is, delaying harder decisions. And if the restaurant fails anyway, the holders become unsecured creditors.

In short, it pulls future revenue forward without fixing the underlying shortfall, creating a deeper cash-flow hole later.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: Selling gift certificates during a severe slump brings in immediate cash, but financially it acts like borrowing against future sales rather than earning true revenue. Every certificate sold creates an unearned-revenue liability on the balance sheet—an obligation to provide meals later. Struggling restaurants typically burn that upfront cash right away to cover overdue rent, utilities, payroll, and vendor bills instead of holding reserves. The crunch hits when customers return to redeem those certificates: the restaurant must pay fresh out-of-pocket costs for ingredients, beverages, and kitchen and service labor while collecting zero new cash at the register. Worse, certificate redemptions can displace full-paying diners from limited tables during peak hours, starving a fragile recovery of desperately needed liquidity. If the certificates were sold with promotional discounts or bonus value to spur quick sales—or if food and wage costs rise before redemption—the restaurant's already thin margins shrink further or even turn negative, transforming short-term cash relief into a deeper solvency crisis.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Selling gift certificates brings in cash now, but it isn't revenue yet. It's a liability. The restaurant has taken money for meals it still has to serve, and it will pay for the food, labor and overhead on those meals later, when it may be just as short of cash. In effect it is borrowing from future customers. During a slump the cash usually goes straight to rent, payroll and suppliers, so nothing is set aside to cover redemptions.

Discounts make it worse. Rescue promotions like "pay $80, get $100" turn this into expensive borrowing at an effective interest rate of 25% or more, and it gets repaid in food and labor. When the cards are redeemed, those diners pay little or no new money, so the meals they eat bring in far less cash than meals sold to paying guests. That hits right as the business is trying to recover.

People who buy cards to support a struggling place also tend to actually use them, so the restaurant can't count on many going unspent. If it fails anyway, cardholders become unpaid creditors, which can bring legal exposure and damage the owners' reputation.
